articles.title: Make Authorization Fence an Invariant Before a Side Lane Reopens the Attempt
articles.excerpt: I replayed a four-event trace on paper before I trusted a side-lane retry classifier at all. The planner had already sealed compensation when the side lane finally returned its late yes answer. A naiv…
articles.body: I replayed a four-event trace on paper before I trusted a side-lane retry classifier at all. The planner had already sealed compensation when the side lane finally returned its late yes answer. A naive merger treated that late yes as fresh permission to reopen the already sealed attempt. Would you really let one delayed label rewrite a closed attempt after compensation had already landed? That order is the whole review, not a footnote I can patch later with a longer timeout. I am treating retry authorization as an append that must carry an open generation fence token. If the fence does not match the live attempt, the log rejects the label and leaves the seal untouched. Why would a slower lane earn more authority than the path that already closed the books?

articles.title: Where Did My Data Go? Benchmarking LLMs as Data Pipeline Detectives
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Every data engineer has gotten this ticket at least once. Someone from sales writes that Umbrella Corp is right there in the CRM but missing…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge What I Benchmarked Every data engineer has gotten this ticket at least once. Someone from sales writes that Umbrella Corp is right there in the CRM but missing from the dashboard, and could you please check where it went, ideally by the end of the day. Nobody knows why, that's the whole point of the ticket. Between the CRM and the dashboard there is a pipeline that ingests the record, extracts the company name, merges duplicates and filters some of them out, and the record could have been lost at any of these steps. So you go digging through the logs, half of which were rotated out last Tuesday, and there in the final table you find "Umbrella Corporation Inc". Is that our Umbrella? Maybe. Probably?

articles.title: Staged Retrieval Relevance Tuning for Private Knowledge Managers (and Why It Holds)
articles.excerpt: For a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way into the answer. That shape is also prac…
articles.body: For a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way into the answer. That shape is also practical for a gaming catalog that aggregates listings from several feeds: index the records once, narrow candidates with metadata, then ask a bounded vector query instead of letting one enormous search decide everything. Short answer: define the retrieval contract first, keep ingestion/query/citation observable as separate stages, and tune against a small set of representative documents and known failures. The storage choice matters, but an unmeasured relevance policy matters more.

But if you're building React applications, implementing browser-signal collection and managing its lifecycle can quickly become repetitive. What if you could encapsulate that functionality in a reusable React hook and use it wherever you need it? articles.title: CVE-2026-104286: Fortinet FortiMail Path Traversal Vulnerability — Analysis & Mitigation
articles.excerpt: On October 1, 2026, Fortinet published advisory FG-IR-26-175 for a vulnerability already being exploited against real customer appliances: CVE-2026-104286, a path traversal flaw in FortiMail that lets…
articles.body: On October 1, 2026, Fortinet published advisory FG-IR-26-175 for a vulnerability already being exploited against real customer appliances: CVE-2026-104286 , a path traversal flaw in FortiMail that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files to the appliance's underlying system through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Rated CVSS 9.8 and listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, this is a zero-day in the truest sense — Fortinet's own Product Security team discovered it while investigating attacks already in progress. FortiMail sits in front of your organization's email flow, which makes this one of the worst places a file-write primitive can land. Here is my full analysis of the bug, the attack chain, and exactly what to do about it.

articles.title: The Server That Robbed Its Own Bank
articles.excerpt: In 2019, a single request stole the personal data of over 100 million people from one of the biggest banks in America. No malware. No stolen password. No one kicked down a door. The attacker just aske…
articles.body: In 2019, a single request stole the personal data of over 100 million people from one of the biggest banks in America. No malware. No stolen password. No one kicked down a door. The attacker just asked a server a question, and the server, trying to be helpful, answered with the keys to the vault. The bug behind it is called SSRF , and once you see how it works, you start noticing the setup for it everywhere. I spent this week learning it hands-on, and I want to walk you through it the way it finally made sense to me, with that real breach as the destination. First, Forget "Breaking In" When most people imagine a server getting hacked, they picture someone forcing their way inside. SSRF is the opposite of that, and that's exactly why it's so easy to miss. You never get in.

This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site.
